name: Lixisenatide

lead: Lixisenatide (Lyxumia, Adlyxin) is a once-daily GLP-1 injection for type 2 diabetes, approved in the EU in 2013 and the US in 2016. In fat-loss discussion it appears as an older member of the GLP-1 class with a slight weight effect.

It activates GLP-1 receptors, boosting insulin release when glucose is high and slowing gastric emptying, which lowers appetite after meals and nudges intake and weight down. In the ELIXA trial it did not increase cardiovascular events relative to placebo.

paras: It is prescribed as a daily injection for diabetes, and is also sold combined with insulin glargine as Soliqua. It is not approved for obesity and has largely been replaced by longer-acting agents.
Nausea and vomiting are common; pancreatitis and allergic reactions are rarer. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Lixisenatide is a short-acting daily GLP-1 injection that lowers appetite after meals, giving a slight weight reduction toward a leaner body. Diabetes trials showed small weight reductions, and it plays a minor role next to newer GLP-1 drugs.

lead: Lixisenatide (Lyxumia in the EU, Adlyxin in the US) is a once-daily injectable short-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes, developed by Zealand Pharma and licensed to Sanofi in 2003.[1] It was approved in the EU in February 2013 and in the US in July 2016.[1]

In the ELIXA trial of patients with type 2 diabetes and a recent acute coronary event, it did not increase cardiovascular events relative to placebo.[2] Its weight effect is modest and it is not approved for obesity. It is also marketed combined with insulin glargine as Soliqua.[3]

paras: It is used as an adjunct to diet and exercise in type 2 diabetes; in the EU its use is limited to combination with insulin therapy.[1] The Soliqua combination is indicated for adults with type 2 diabetes.[3]

Reported effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache and dizziness; rarer events include pancreatitis, anaphylaxis and hypoglycemia with insulin or sulfonylureas.[1][3] It is not recommended in people with gastroparesis.[1]

Sanofi withdrew its first US application in September 2013 to await cardiovascular safety data, and resubmitted in 2015.[1] Protection lapsed in 2020.[1] Sources reviewed describe the product as discontinued in some markets without detail.

ELIXA randomized 6,068 patients with a recent acute coronary event.[2][4] A meta-analysis of GLP-1 agonist cardiovascular outcome trials assessed the class.[5] A mixed-treatment comparison examined efficacy and safety across GLP-1 agonists.[6] A 2024 phase 2 trial tested lixisenatide in early Parkinson's disease.[7] Preclinical work shows the drug crosses the blood-brain barrier.[8]

timeline.event: EU approval; first US filing withdrawn.[1]
